FAO guidelines and geospatial application for agroforestry
suitability mapping: case study of Ranchi, Jharkhand state
of India
Firoz Ahmad . Laxmi Goparaju . Abdul Qayum
Received: 7 July 2017 / Accepted: 21 October 2017 / Published online: 27 October 2017
 Springer Science+Business Media B.V. 2017
Abstract
Agroforestry has potential for achieving
agricultural sustainability having capacity of optimiz-
ing its productivity by mitigating climate change
impacts. The aim was to ﬁnd such land patches which
can be potentially mapped as suitable and fertile for
agroforestry projects and to ﬁnd out land-use systems
which can play a pivotal role in poverty eradication
and climate change mitigation. The study aims for
applying geo-spatial technology towards visualizing
various land, soil, climate and topographical data to
reveal trends and interrelationships and to ﬁnd a
nutrient availability and agroforestry suitability map.
FAO based land suitability criteria was adopted to
generate agroforestry suitability maps based upon
scientiﬁcally evaluated weight factors at GIS platform
by integrating layers of LULC, NDVI, wetness factor,
elevation, slope percent, drainage, watershed, rainfall,
organic carbon, pH and nutrient status. About 6% of
land is under cultivation of pure agriculture whereas
the study area has agroforestry suitability of 32.8% of
total area. Block wise agroforestry suitability reveals
highly suitable percentage for Rahe, Bundu and
Namkum blocks as 79.1, 56.5 and 1.1%, respectively.
Based on high suitability percentage Rahe block
among all should be prioritized. Therefore, if there is
scientiﬁc planning with adequate technical inputs, the
area can achieve tremendous scope for tribal and rural
people in generating their livelihood. Such ﬁnding
may work as guiding tool for the policymakers
towards allocation of fund for agroforestry projects.
The advance GIS modeling software has the potential
to map such area logically and meaningfully.
Keywords
Agroforestry  Digital elevation model
(DEM)  FAO  GIS  Land suitability  Nutrient status 
Remote Sensing
Introduction
Land evaluation is formally deﬁned as ‘the analysis of
land performance when used for a speciﬁed purpose,
involving the execution and interpretation of surveys
and studies of land forms, soils, vegetation, climate
and other characteristics of land in order to identify
and make a comparison of promising kinds of land use
in terms of suitability to the objectives of the
evaluation’ (FAO 1976). Population is a direct driver
of environmental degradation when it exceeds the
threshold limits of the support system say carrying
capacity. Poverty is considered as both cause and
effect of such degradation. The relationship between

MirzapurUttar Pradesh, India

Department of Environment and Forest, Govt. of
Arunachal Pradesh, Itanagar, India
e-mail: qayum.iitk@gmail.com
123
Agroforest Syst (2019) 93:531–544
DOI 10.1007/s10457-017-0145-y
native_page_text.2:
pressure due to population and environmental degra-
dation were reviewed in studies on rangeland degra-
dation (Tiffen et al. 1994), soil fertility decline
(Phillips-Howard
and
Lyon
1994),
deforestation
(Fairhead and Leach 1996), soil and water resources
degradation (Reij et al. 1996) and plant biomass
production (Mortimore et al. 1999).
One of the most important challenges faced by the
developing nations is producing food, fuel and fodder
in quantities so as to fulﬁll the demand of burgeoning
population. It is also a necessity to ensure that the
fertility of land resources that are directly or indirectly
utilized in cultivating crops should be maintained and
improved thereupon. Therefore, it is important to
increase productivity and enhance the quality of eco-
system by adopting several conservation measures.
Agroforestry combines agriculture and forestry
technologies to create diverse, proﬁtable, and sustain-
able land-use systems and having capability to reduce
poverty and make resilience towards climate changes.
It is a land management and farming system which not
only aims for producing food from marginal agricul-
tural land but also to maintain and improve the quality
of environment substantially (Thangataa and Hilde-
brand 2012). Agroforestry has number of beneﬁtsto its
credit for farmers, society and environment. For
instance, it can enhance soil fertility, improve farm
household resilience and at the same time provide
additional products for sale or local consumption as a
cost-effective means to enhance food security (Tilman
et al. 2011), provide livelihood beneﬁts (Islam et al.
2015) while at the same time contributing to climate
change adaptation and mitigation (Thorlakson and
Neufeldt 2012) to conserve and enhance the quality of
eco-system (Hernandez et al. 2016; Asbjornsen et al.
2014) to conserving biodiversity (McNeely 2004; Jose
2012; Ramos et al. 2015). Therefore, the agroforestry
suitability evaluation of land is pertinent asagro-
forestry being one of the future technological innova-
tions will be inevitable in meeting food demands for
the global increase in population (Lal 2000).
Why agroforestry suitability mapping using
geospatial technology?
Geospatial technology and its methods for land
evaluation can be potentially harnessed in variety of
applications ranging from resource assessment to land
evaluation and land use planning, using tools such as
data visualization, data analysis and evaluation of
scenarios (Montesano et al. 2009). Free accessibility
to imagery and online datasets availability increasing
day by day (Ploton et al. 2012) and widely it is used for
Geographic Information System (GIS) based model-
ing. GIS platform has become a powerful desktop
system for storing and managing geo-referenced data,
and conducting spatial analysis. Geographic databases
can be built and new data from surveys can be
imported using Global Positioning System (GPS)
technology. Additional layers can be created using
combinations of existing layers by employing tools
such as buffering, cross tabulation, classiﬁcation,
interpolation, surface density modeling and other
analytical functions. Further analysis can make use
of statistical techniques coupled to GIS (Bydekerke
et al. 1998). The available GIS methods are usually
combined with expert knowledge or production mod-
eling to support studies such as land suitability
assessment (Bouma et al. 1993). Spatial parameters
such as land, soil, climate and topographical and land
cover together can be used for land evaluation which
can identify suitability locations for agroforestry
practices to resolve farmers, landowner and commu-
nity concerns. A simple overview of the GIS based
agroforestry suitability assessment process can be
illustrated through schematic ﬂowchart.
By selecting appropriate data with the suitable spa-
tial resolution, this assessment process can be used at
any scale for planning agroforestry practices. The
most remarkable beneﬁt of this suitability mapping is
the ability to combine different assessments to deter-
mine sites where multiple objectives can be achieved.
Suitability assessments have been previously used to
identify locations for different land uses such as
landﬁlls, wildlife habitat, and residential development
(McHarg 1995). Although GIS and the suitability
mapping towards environmental protection applica-
tions has been commonly used (Ellis et al. 2000)
whereas this technology has yet to be used extensively
in agroforestry (Bentrup and Leininger 2002).
Few researcher and scientist have evaluated land
for various agroforestry application based on FAO
guideline. Ritung et al. (2007) used climatic, soil and
topographical data and evaluated land based on FAO
guideline of Aceh Barat District of Indonesia and
recommended land suitable for various agroforestry
crops. Dengiz (2013) carried out GIS modeling and
land suitability assessment in the Central Anatolian
532
Agroforest Syst (2019) 93:531–544
123
native_page_text.3:
region of Turkey for rice cultivation. The result
showed that 55.5% of the study area is highly or
moderately suitable for rice cultivation, whereas 34%
of that area is unsuitable for rice cultivation due to soil
and topographic conditions. Reisner et al. (2007)
studied land evaluation for agroforestry for Europe in
GIS domain and have proposed silvoarable agro-
forestry (SAF) which has the capacity to reduce the
risk of soil erosion, nitrate leaching and enhance the
landscape diversity.
Further, Kihoro et al. (2013) carried out study in
Kirinyaga, Embu and Mberee counties in Kenya and
evaluated land suitability analysis using biophysical
variables of soil, climate and topography for rice
growing sites using a multi-criteria evaluation and GIS
approach based on FAO guideline and found that the
potential area for rice growing is 86,364 ha and out of
this only 12% is under rice cultivation. Yedage et al.
(2013) has evaluated land suitability on FAO guide-
line towards horticulture crop (pomegranate) in Sola-
pur district of Maharashtra, India using multi-criteria
approach. The parameters used for the evaluation were
slope, soil pH, soil organic carbon, soil NPK, soil
texture, soil electric conductivity, soil depth, ground
water availability and the present land use land cover
(LULC). Around 27% area is highly and 18% is
moderately suitable for pomegranate cultivation.
Ahmad et al. (2017) evaluated land of Chakard-
harpur subdivision of West Singhbhum district of
Jharkhand, India based on FAO guideline towards
agroforestry suitability utilizing the weight and
ranks approach in GIS modeling. The parameter
utilized for generating nutrient availability map were
soil nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K),
organic carbon (C), pH and sulphur (S) whereas
parameter used for agroforestry suitability were wet-
ness, rainfall, slope, elevation, and nutrient availabil-
ity map. The total open area land was identiﬁed 42.4%
out of which 21.6% area was found to have high
suitability towards agroforestry. Ahmad and Goparaju
(2017a, b) studied land evaluation for Agroforestry of
Dumka and Palamu districts of Jharkhand, India based
upon FAO guideline. In both study GIS modeling
approach was exploited and parameter used were
wetness, rainfall, slope, elevation, and nutrient avail-
ability map. The study reveals in Dumka district that
total open area land grids were 3421 out of which 50%
of grid was found to be highly suitable for agroforestry
whereas in Palamu district that total open area land
grids were 3334 out of which 62% of grid was found to
be highly suitable towards agroforestry.
The present study aims for applying Remote
Sensing (RS) and GIS towards visualizing additional
spatial dimensions of land, soil, climate and topo-
graphical data to reveal trends and interrelationships
and to achieve a nutrient status map leading to
agroforestry suitability mapping. At the end, agro-
forestry maps were evaluated based upon the LULC of
the area.
The study area
The study was carried out in three blocks of Ranchi
district namely Namkum, Bunduand Rahe, which
form part of Swarnrekha basin of Jharkhand state of
India, having latitudes 2306014.400N to 2323010.400N
and longitudes 851301.400E to 85440 46.900 E (Fig. 1).
The altitude varies from 361 to 748 m for Namkun,
230–668 m for Bundu and 226–620 m for Rahe
blocks from the mean sea level. The climate remains
humid subtropical. The annual rainfall in the region
varies from 1200 to 1400 mm of which 75–80% is
received during the monsoon periods June to Septem-
ber months. Temperature is lowest during December
and January and maximum during April and May with
mean maximum, summer temperatures range from 20
to 43 C, while winter temperature varies from 2 to
25 C. The forests of this area can be best described as
tropical dry deciduous, tropical moist deciduous, dry
Sal and moist Sal (Champion and Seth 1968). Shorea
robusta (sal) is the dominant species whereas other
few predominant species are Butea monosperma,
Madhuca latifolia, Diospyrossp, Phyllanthus emblica,
Azadirachta indica, Dalbergia sissoo, Acacia arabica,
Zizyphus jujuba and Mangifera indica. Geologically
the area contains Archean granites, gneisses and
schists whereas soil orders mainly Entisols, Incepti-
sols and Alﬁsols are found. Alﬁsols are the dominant
soil occupying around 71% of the area. Granite and
Geneissic plateau surface are commonly dominated
with red soil. The soils of upland are found to be
shallow to medium depth, reddish in colour, well to
excessively drained, sensitive to erosion with low
water holding capacity and high permeability whereas
in lowland soils are grey in colour, neutral in reaction,
high clay content and high fertility status. As per FSI
(2015) report Ranchi district has 27% as forest area out

Materials and methods
Data used for suitability mapping was from Landsat
OLI (Path-140, Row-44; dated 23-12-2013) with
spatial resolution of 30 m. The data was taken in
month of December as it falls in the winter season
where all vegetation is clearly visible (including
forest) as well as during that time cloud cover is least.
Therefore, visibility eventually gets better and image
capturing becomes prominent. The forest in the region
is mostly evergreen and deciduous. During summer
the trees shed their leaves, hence not suitable for forest
area interpretation. Getting cloud free data during
rainy season is difﬁcult. Post monsoon or winter
season has full foliage or trees are in full bloom which
is important for forest area delineation. The projection
parameter was WGS84 UTM zone 45. The geo-
referenced satellite data was downloaded from portal
of United States Geological Survey (USGS) in 11
bands. Later, all the bands were layer stacked to
produce a composite image which was converted into
IMG format for further analysis. The bands used for
analysis were NIR (5), Red (4), and green (3). ERDAS
imaging (V. 9.1) was used for image processing and
ArcGIS (V. 10.1) for spatial analysis. ASTER DEM
with 30 m resolution was downloaded from USGS

LULC classiﬁcation
The visual interpretation technique was used to give
training sets to assess major land cover classiﬁcations.
Supervised classiﬁcation (maximum likelihood tech-
niques) was executed to delineate twelve classes by
providing 10–15 signature of each class over the entire
images. Image alarm was used to validate the signa-
ture. Image alarm is the step for evaluation (error of
omission and commission) of signature provided by
the user for delineating any class while doing the
image classiﬁcation. It was observed that few areas of
agriculture were mixed in forest class, to clearly
demarcate those areas forest mask was generated from
false colour composite (FCC) and utilized. Vegetated
areas in non-forest mask were assigned agriculture
class. The ﬁnal classes were water, agriculture mix,
settlement/grassland,
fallow,
barren,
pure
forest,
degraded forest and open forest (Fig. 3). Accuracy
assessment validates quality of the classiﬁed image,
which is important step in generating thematic map
from satellite data. The accuracy assessment was
carried out by generating random points in Landsat
image. The overall classiﬁcation accuracy and kappa
statistics is generated for classiﬁed output.
Vegetation map-NDVI
The Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI)
is a most commonly used vegetation index and is an
indicator of plant ‘‘greenness’’ or photosynthetic
activity (Rani and Rajiv 2015) NDVI map is generated
for Landsat 8 data using the formula.

Wetness map
The recent research studies towards achieving wetness
map using Landsat image has been scientiﬁcally
recognized and used in various applications. Wetness
is one of the strong parameter which provides

ArcGIS has several modules including Spatial Analyst
for processing vast data sets of which surface sub

source in GIS domain
Ancillary data source at an average of 10 years
(1993–2002) of annual rainfall data was obtained from
Indian water portal (http://www.indiawaterportal.org/
met_data/) and used to generate continuous surface
spatial rainfall pattern by the method of Kriging

rectiﬁed

digitized in each datasets and attributes were assigned
for organic carbon (Fig. 11) and soil pH (Fig. 12).
Nutrient status mapping using GIS modeling
The GIS integrated ﬂow diagram of nutrient status
mapping was done (Fig. 13). GIS layers generated
from ancillary source were used to develop nutrient
availability map by assigning equal weight (Table 2)
to soil primary nutrient N, P and K-parameter which is
essential and equally important for metabolic activi-
ties for plant growth (Fig. 14).
Agroforestry suitability mapping using GIS
modeling
The Food and Agricultural Organization (FAO) has
suggested methods to evaluate suitability of land
(FAO 1976). The geospatial technology with free data
sets online now these days made it easy to evaluate
land to certain purpose. GIS modeling provides huge
opportunity to pool different GIS layer as per its
importance. Similar approach based on FAO guideli-
nes was applied to evaluate land potentiality to

Such data is widely unavailable in developing coun-
tries due to lack of high resolution remote sensing
data, GIS personnel and modern lab facilities.
Agro forestry suitability analysis
Agroforestry land suitability map was produced by
pooling all essential thematic layers such as elevation,
rainfall, wetness, nutrient status, organic carbon, pH,
vegetation and slope percent as per its relative
importance based weight factors (Table 4). Similar
studies were conducted by Ahmad et al. (2017),
Ahmad and Goparaju 2017a, b) for agroforestry
suitability analysis. Suitability map was classiﬁed into
four groups namely highly suitable (S1), moderately
suitable (S2), marginally suitable (S3) and not suit-
able (N) (Table 3; Fig. 15).

Results and discussion
Accuracy assessment in land use/land cover
classes
The accuracy assessment was performed in classiﬁed
LULC image generated from Landsat images of the
year 2013. The overall classiﬁcation accuracy was
90%, whereas kappa statistics was 0.8677.
Agroforestry suitability mapping

High suitability areas
These are the areas with elevation less than 500 m and
having rainfall greater than 1170 mm and relatively
very high wetness. The nutrient status is high with
more than 0.75% organic carbon and soil pH with
range 6.5–5.6. The slope percent is nearly level to
gentle slope (0–5%) with NDVI values very high to
high provides highly favorable condition for plant
growth. It constitutes 31,518 ha (32.8% of total area)
of land. This area is highly fertile and best suitable for
agri-silvi-horticulture system. Agriculture crop spe-
cially paddy crops in low land (locally called don) area
scan be potentially harvested due to adequate avail-
ability of water and moisture during monsoon season.
After monsoon season, the area can have huge
potential for horticulture crop as it retains soil
moisture post-monsoon also. Large piece of uplands
(locally called tar)area with suitable climate and high
nutrient value offers immense potential for diversiﬁ-
cation under horticultural crops such as Mango,
Guava, Litchi, Lemon, Banana, Papaya and Jackfruit,
etc. whereas vegetables such as potato, cauliﬂower,
brinjal, tomato, cabbage, pea, okra, chilly, cucurbits
and sweet pepper etc. Considering the agroforestry
potential and availability of vast area a scientiﬁc
planning need to be done and implemented to realize
horticulture potential. The trees Sisam (Dalbergia
sissoo) Asan (Terminalia tomentosa), Arjun (Termi-
nalia arjuna), Sal (Shorea robusta) trees and Ber
(Zizyphus mauritiana) tree, and Palas (Butea mono-
sperma) can be grown. Further, bamboo can be
suitably cultivated both in undulating hilly areas and

Moderate suitability
These areas were with elevation 500–700 m with
1170–1150 mm rainfall and wetness was relatively
high. The nutrient availability was moderate with
0.75–0.50% organic carbon and soil pH with range
5.5–5.1. The slope was gentle to moderate (5–15%)
with NDVI medium to low and no ease of cultivation
provides moderate favorable condition for plant
growth. It constitutes of 38,822 ha (40.4% of total
area). It is moderately fertile with adequate soil
moisture only during rainy seasons. Soil erosion is
high due to gravitational force component acting
heavily due to moderate slope. There is need of soil
and moisture conservation works including raising
fertility by adding farm yard manure (FYM) and green
manures. A lime treatment is also needed to increase
soil pH. Horticulture crops such as egg plant, carrot,
cauliﬂower cucumber garlic, pepper, tomato and
radish shows poor growth when pH is less than 5.5
(Albert 2013). Soil pH is also important because soil
acidity or alkalinity determines availability of nutrient
up to the plant roots. Nutrients in soil in form of
nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium become avail-
able when these are dissolved in water or soil
moisture.

Marginal suitability
It was found in the region having elevation greater
than 700 m and rainfall less than 1150 mm while
wetness was moderate to low. The nutrient availability
was low having less than 0.50% organic carbon and
soil pH with range 5.0–4.5. The slope varies from
moderate to steep (15–35%) with NDVI values from
low to nil with no ease of cultivation provide poor
favorable condition for plant growth. It constitutes
25,094 ha (26.11% of total area). This area strongly
exhibited poor fertility which needs to be treated by
improving organic carbon by supplying FYM and
green manures along with commercial fertilizers.
Moisture content was relatively very low and sign of
high soil erosion in this area due to steep slope. Thus,
soil and water conservation works are required to
achieve required plant growth. Lime treatment may
also be needed to increase soil pH. Horticulture crop
such as potato and peanut can be grown after lime
treatment and a good growth is possible up to low pH
of 5. This area can be used for dry land farming

land in form of fallow, barren, degraded forest and
open forests can have the potential for agroforestry if it
is properly planned as it falls in moderate agroforestry
suitability class. Agroforestry projects can be adopted
in these lands because of its suitability from high to
moderate class, if some barriers can be resolved
largely related to soil moisture, project funding and
proper technical guidance; it will greatly contribute for
tribal and rural people livelihood. Further, the study is
highly likely to help in poverty eradication in the long
run.
Soil moisture can be retained if in situ moisture
conservation practices such as mulching zero tillage,
ridge and furrow system and strip cropping can be
applied. In the study area around70–80% of rainwater
is being lost through runoff. Therefore, it is also
important to retain rain water as far as possible by
means of different soil and moisture conservation
methods including construction of check dams and
ponds. This will not only recharge downstream but
also provide adequate moisture for the next crop. This
practice can minimize soil erosion and nutrient loss
due to runoff control (http://www.fao.org/docrep/
t1696e/t1696e02.htm). In such rain fed area delin-
eation of watershed, drainage and agroforestry suit-
ability mapping is important to tap maximum rain
water by water conservation management practice and
utilizing the land with its optimum potential for vari-
ous land use at sustainable basis.
Prioritization of blocks based on agroforestry
suitability criteria
Block wise agroforestry suitability with 2011 census
data is given Table 7. Three administrative blocks of
the study area were evaluated for its suitability
towards agroforestry and it was found that Rahe,
Bundu and Namkum block comprised of 79.1, 56.5
and 1.1%, respectively of land area in highly suit-
able (S1) category. Therefore, Rahe block among all
should be prioritized for agroforestry projects. This
block consists of 39.1% schedule caste (SC) and
schedule tribe (ST) population when compared with
total block population whereas this block consist 9496
cultivators and 13,663 agricultural laborers which will
be directly beneﬁted if prioritized.
Bundu block is second in prioritization, which
consists of 55.4% SC and ST population whereas ST
population is 48.1% of the block population. Due to
concentrated tribal population, their poverty and
livelihood is major thrust in rural area to be resolved
by involving them in various ongoing and future
livelihood or forest conservation programs. Agro-
forestry program must be incorporated in future

degraded forest based upon its suitability in conjunc-
tion with soil and water conservation program at
watershed level. Around 90% of the Bundu block falls
in one watershed for its soil moisture requirements

Namkum block consists of moderate suitability
(S2) with 48.5%. It has 65.1% SC and ST population
where ST population alone is 60% of the block. This
area needed more soil treatment because of its acidity
needed to be ameliorated with lime/dolomite where
acidity is high. Organic carbon in general in this area is
found to be low and therefore it shall be by FYM and
green manures. Areas with slope greater than 5% shall
be treated with soil and water conservation practices at
watershed level with efﬁcient drainage management
including brushwood check-dams. In dry land agri-
culture dust mulch is highly recommended practice for
water conservation (Hegde 1995). Soil erosion and
nutrient deﬁciency in such slope is common due to
high runoff and situation deteriorates further with
increase of slope. This area can be used for agro-

Conclusion
This study has utilized various themes pulling together
from diverse sources of information which are related
to various agroforestry systems. Computer based
various datasets and its logical analysis using geospa-
tial tools such RS and GIS have greatly facilitated the
decision-making process to achieve the goals agro-
forestry suitability mapping for users including
landowners, foresters, and farmers. The government
has initiated many projects for the poor and tribal
people/farmers for practicing integrated watershed
management plan for harnessing agroforestry poten-
tial. There is a need to identify the potentially
suitable land for agroforestry and implement or divert
the current projects there to utilize it signiﬁcantly
which will certainly enhance the livelihood. Agro-
forestry is like hanging fruits which need to be
exploited scientiﬁcally. Bearing it in mind, India has
adopted agroforestry policy and aimed to increase
farmer’s income to double digit by the year 2022.
Agroforestry is considered as the backbone of
marginal farming for a self-reliant and sustainable
agriculture. It has the potential for meeting the
extreme challenges of food security, while environ-
mental security is a prime beneﬁt of agroforestry
systems. It is evident from the results that one-fourth
of the total land (which is not fully utilized) of the
study is likely to have agroforestry practice potential
as it falls in high suitable category (S1), if limitations
such as soil moisture, adequate funding and proper
technical guidance is resolved. The ﬁndings and
suitability map can be incorporated with various
ongoing and future land based management program
which will produce sustainable beneﬁts to the thriving
rural and tribal people in poverty alleviation by raising
livelihood opportunities. There is necessity to evaluate
the land capability and its potential towards its
suitability for different crop/trees productivity. There
is a need to incorporate such data by the policy makers
for future land planning and management towards its
suitability to the crop and trees. This research high-
lights tremendous ability of remote sensing (coarse
resolution data) as well as spatial dimension of land,
soil, climate and topographical data integration under
GIS domain, which proves its huge potential for
evaluating land capability and its productivity.
